bg: amos, book of

The book of the prophecies of Amos seems to be divided into four principal portions closely connected together. (1) From 1:1 to 2:3 he denounces the sins of the nations bordering on Israel and Judah. (2) From 2:4 to 6:14 he describes the state of those two kingdoms, especially, the former. (3) From 7:1 to 9:10 he relates his visit to Bethel, and sketches the impending punishment of Israel. At last
Edom

There are many prophecies concerning Edom (Isa. 34:5, 6; Jer. 49:7-18; Ezek. 25:13; 35:1-15; Joel 3:19; Amos 1:11; Obad.; Mal. 1:3, 4) which have been remarkably fulfilled. The present desolate condition of that land is a standing testimony to the inspiration of these prophecies.
Damascus

The Syrians were at length subdued by the Assyrians, the city of Damascus was taken and destroyed, and the inhabitants carried captive into Assyria (2 Kings 16:7-9; comp. Isa. 7:8). In this, prophecy was fulfilled (Isa. 17:1; Amos 1:4; Jer. 49:24).
Gilead
Hill of testimony, (Gen. 31:21), a mountainous region east of Jordan. From its mountainous character it is called "the mount of Gilead" (Gen. 31:25).
ch.s: Judgments against the Syrians, Philistines, Tyrians, Edomites, and Ammonites (Matthew Henry Concise). People named: Amos, Uzziah, Jeroboam, Hazael. Places: Damascus, Gaza, Tyrus, Edom, Ammon.
q: Read verses 1–4 (Opens: “The words of Amos, who was among the herdmen…”). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 5–8 (Opens: “I will break also the bar of Damascus, and…”), what do you learn about judgment?
Verse 11 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Ezekiel 25:12–14. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Amos’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of sin and repentance in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Amos?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.a: Let the seriousness of God's judgment move you to examine your ways and to pray for others.
ch.mh: GOD employed a shepherd, a herdsman, to reprove and warn the people. Those to whom God gives abilities for his services, ought not to be despised for their origin, or their employment.

Bashan

Light soil, first mentioned in Gen. 14:5, where it is said that Chedorlaomer and his confederates "smote the Rephaim in Ashteroth," where Og the king of Bashan had his residence. At the time of Israel's entrance into the Promised Land, Og came out against them, but was utterly routed (Num. 21:33-35; Deut. 3:1-7).

Fort, one of the four cities founded by Nimrod (Gen. 10:10). It is the modern Niffer, a lofty mound of earth and rubbish situated in the marshes on the left, i.e., the east, bank of the Euphrates, but 30 miles distant from its present course, and about 60 miles south-south-east from Babylon.

His name occurs in Scripture only in 2 Kings 13:13; 14:16, 23, 27, 28, 29; 15:1, 8; 1 Chr. 5:17; Hos. 1:1; Amos 1:1; 7:9, 10, 11. In all other passages it is Jeroboam the son of Nebat that is meant.

A chaplet, the original seat of the Philistines (Deut. 2:23; Jer. 47:4; Amos 9:7). The name is found written in hieroglyphics in the temple of Kom Ombos in Upper Egypt.
Carmel

A park; generally with the article, "the park." (1.)
